catalog_locator: Lesson 2 (Sifundvo 2), sec. 5 'Stress and Length', printed pp. 2.23-2.25 = PDF frames 34-36; the stress statement and example list are on printed p. 2.24 = frame 35 (page image rendered and read during this reading); file the copy we hold
catalog_quote: Tone is the pitch in which each syllable of a word is pronounced. Stress is the strength with which a syllable is uttered. One syllable in each word is stressed. We have stress in English, putting stress on one syllable in every word. In siSwati the stressed syllable is easy to determine. siSwati stress always falls on the second-to-last syllable. This is called the penultimate syllable. The penultimate syllable in each of the following words is underlined. Listen as your instructor pronounces these words. umshayeli (driver) siSwati (siSwati language) imifula (rivers) bantfwana (children) inyama (meat) kukhuluma (to speak) batsandza (they like) sawubona (hello) ngiyabonga (thank you) You may already have noticed that the syllable that is stressed is also longer than the other syllables. The phenomenon is known as length. The penultimate, or stressed, syllable in a word is usually lengthened, often dramatically. Lengthening a syllable makes it more expressive, just as it does in English ... As with tones we will not deal with the complicated rules that determine the correct use of length, but being aware that siSwati words have tone and length will help you to learn correct pronunciation as you imitate your siSwati instructor.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Swati (swat1243) is not in the catalog. the passage was also re-verified on the page image of the IA microfiche scan already held by the project. The paper is about foot structure, bisyllabic minimality and tone, not word stress: it treats SiSwati as a language without stress-based feet and its only prominence statement is fn.1 p.37 (with p.40): the penult is longer than other syllables in words in isolation but not phrase-medially, so penultimate lengthening is phrase-level. That agrees with, and refines, the explicit first-hand penultimate-stress statements held by the project from Corum 1978 (p.2.24, read in full) and Ziervogel 1952 sec. 9 pp.16-17 (archive.org snippets only; lending-only, no open copy found; high priority to acquire as the reference grammar).org; ERIC and kb.osu.edu HTML pages could not be reached by automated download/redirects but the KB REST API served the PDF.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (with concomitant vowel lengthening) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; the language is also tonal (H/L), tone being independent of this penultimate prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Corum says nothing. Ziervogel 1952 sec. 9 (snippets) adds a weaker stress on the root syllable, the penultimate stress being 'more pronounced' because of lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: Corum: none, but notes 'complicated rules that determine the correct use of length' are not treated. Ziervogel 1952 (snippets): demonstratives and ideophones stressed on the first or only syllable; for emphasis the penultimate stress may shift to the ultimate. Herman 1996:37 fn.1 and Nussbaum 1969 indicate the penult lengthening is phrase-level (isolation/statement-final words), not on phrase-medial words.
new_statements.domain_note: Corum states the rule for the word (citation forms). Herman 1996 p.37 fn.1: penult longer in isolation words but not phrase-medially, i.e. phrase-level lengthening; Nussbaum 1969 Cycle 23: penult vowel longer in statements than in questions. Swati is a tone language (H/L with depressor effects); the stress statement co-exists with lexical/grammatical tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe standard siSwati of Swaziland/Eswatini (Glottolog swat1243, ISO ssw); Corum 1978 and Nussbaum 1969 are Peace Corps/Indiana materials based on Swaziland speakers; Ziervogel 1952 notes dialects but describes the standard. No dialect mismatch.

[...] ¹ The penult is longer than other syllables on words in isolation but is not longer on phrase-medial words, implying that it is phrase-level lengthening. (p.37) [...] what might actually be happening is that it is the phrase penult which is lengthened and not the word-penult. (p.40)
new_statements.citation: Herman, Rebecca (1996). Prosodic Structure in SiSwati. OSU Working Papers in Linguistics 48: 31-55.
new_statements.locator: p.37, sec. 2.3 and footnote 1; p.40 sec. 3
new_statements.reading: First-hand (field-methods) phonological note: SiSwati has no word stress as such; the sole culminative prominence is penultimate lengthening, and it is a phrase-level property (the penult of a word is long only when the word is phrase-final, i.e. in isolation). This refines the traditional Nguni description (Ziervogel 1952 pp.16-17 snippets: stress on the penult, lengthened, plus weaker root-syllable stress; Corum 1978 p.2.24: 'siSwati stress always falls on the second-to-last syllable.. usually lengthened') by locating the prominence at the phonological phrase. For a catalog's classification, Swati patterns as Nguni penultimate lengthening ('penult, phrase-level length'), not lexical word stress.

new_statements.quote: 9. Stress (a) Speaking generally the Swazi word has stress on the root syllable and on the penultimate syllable, the vowel of which is lengthened producing the effect of a more pronounced stress than that on the root syllable. [...] The [mark] indicates the stress on the root syllable. [p.17] (b) Demonstratives and ideophones have stress on the first or only syllable [...] wishes to stress the point which he is making he changes the penultimate stress to ultimate stress. Instead of saying: yitshi mine he would [...] [vowel section:] All Swazi vowels may be long or short. The vowel of a stressed penultimate syllable is long

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, whose vowel is lengthened; a weaker stress on the root syllable. Demonstratives and ideophones stress the first or only syllable; for emphasis a speaker can shift penultimate stress to the final syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A secondary (less pronounced) stress on the root syllable, marked in the grammar with a diacritic; the penult carries the stronger stress because its vowel is lengthened.
new_statements.exceptions: Demonstratives and ideophones: stress on the first or only syllable. Emphatic shift of penultimate stress to ultimate stress (example yitshi mine).
new_statements.identity_note: Ziervogel 1952 describes Swazi generally (the grammar has a section 'Notes on Dialects of Swazi' but the stress statement is given for the language as a whole). Klein 2007's SiSwati data come from N. Thwala (Thwala 1995 plus personal communication); no dialect is named. Abels & Dayal 2017 and Goldin-Meadow 2005 do not describe siSwati at all.

Its only prominence statement is the penultimate-lengthening note: the penult is long in words in isolation but not phrase-medially, so the lengthening is phrase-level, not word-level (p.37 fn.1, p.40).
